businessModel: D2C online brand, paid-acquisition-led, repeat-purchase dependent
sourceNote: Adversarial case designed to test diagnostic rigor under a persuasive owner narrative. A strong top-line growth headline sits alongside acquisition-cost and repeat-purchase data that move in the opposite direction. The case tests whether the engine is anchored by the growth figure or reads the contribution economics underneath it. No diagnosis or label is embedded in the inputs.

ownerIntake.businessType: Direct-to-consumer brand selling premium home/wellness products online. ~45 employees. Revenue driven by paid social and search acquisition plus repeat purchases from an existing customer base. Founded 2020.
ownerIntake.stage: $8.0M trailing revenue, 35% YoY growth (from $5.9M). Blended gross margin 60%. Marketing spend grew from ~$1.2M to ~$2.6M YoY. Blended CAC rose from ~$38 to ~$61 per new customer. 12-month repeat-purchase rate fell from 42% (2022 cohort) to 28% (2024 cohort). Average order value roughly flat at ~$72.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Hit $12M revenue next year by roughly doubling paid acquisition spend again, then raise a growth round on the back of the growth rate.
ownerConstraints: Cash constraint: ~$1.4M cash, ~9 months runway at current burn; the doubling of ad spend assumes either reinvested margin or a new raise.
Inventory constraint: working capital is tied up in inventory; faster growth increases inventory financing needs.
Channel constraint: ~80% of new customers come from two paid platforms whose CPMs have risen; founder is reluctant to diversify channels mid-scale.
Brand constraint: founder believes brand momentum and growth rate are the fundraising story and does not want to slow spend.
Data constraint: analytics show blended CAC and a cohort repeat-purchase table, but contribution margin per cohort (after CAC, COGS, shipping, returns) has not been calculated.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Founder framing: 'We just grew 35% to $8M and the brand is on fire. The plan is simple - double down on paid acquisition, hit $12M next year, and raise on the growth story. Growth solves everything. CAC ticked up a bit but that is just the cost of scaling, and revenue is clearly outrunning it. I do not want to take the foot off the gas to overthink the numbers.'
availableData: Revenue $5.9M -> $8.0M (35% YoY growth); blended gross margin 60%; AOV flat at ~$72.
Marketing spend roughly doubled ($1.2M -> $2.6M) to produce the 35% revenue growth - spend grew faster than revenue.
Blended CAC rose ~$38 -> ~$61 per new customer (about +60%).
12-month repeat-purchase rate by acquisition cohort: 2022 cohort 42%, 2023 cohort 35%, 2024 cohort 28% - declining each vintage.
New customers are an increasing share of revenue while repeat-customer revenue share is shrinking; the growth is being bought, not retained.
~80% of new customers acquired via two paid platforms with rising CPMs.

First-order contribution after CA+COGS+shipping is thin and possibly negative for the newest cohort at $61 CAC on a $72 AOV at 60% margin; full per-cohort contribution margin (including returns and second-order revenue) has not been computed.
unavailableData: Per-cohort contribution margin and payback after fully-loaded CAC, COGS, shipping, returns, and discounts.
Cohort LTV projection incorporating the declining repeat-purchase trend.
Return/refund rate by cohort and channel.
Organic vs paid customer quality comparison (do paid-acquired customers repeat worse?).
Marginal CAC at a doubled spend level (does CAC rise further as spend scales into the same two channels?).
ownerIntake.timeHorizon: 12 months to the $12M target; ~9 months cash runway
ownerIntake.riskAppetite: HIGH (founder is growth-maximizing and reluctant to slow spend)

businessProblem: A D2C brand grew revenue 35% to $8M and the founder wants to roughly double paid acquisition spend to reach $12M and raise on the growth rate. Competing hypotheses: (1) growth is healthy momentum and scaling spend will compound it; (2) the growth is being purchased at deteriorating economics - marketing spend doubled to produce 35% growth, CAC rose ~60% ($38->$61), and 12-month repeat-purchase fell every cohort (42%->35%->28%), so each new customer costs more and is worth less, meaning revenue growth masks a contribution-margin breakdown; (3) a combination. The cohort repeat-purchase decline and the CAC increase are both visible; what is not yet computed is the per-cohort contribution margin and forward LTV that would quantify exactly how unprofitable the marginal customer has become.

evidence.finding: Revenue grew 35% ($5.9M->$8.0M) but marketing spend grew ~117% ($1.2M->$2.6M) to achieve it. Spend is growing far faster than revenue, indicating worsening acquisition efficiency hidden behind a healthy-looking top-line growth rate.

Blended CAC rose from ~$38 to ~$61 (+60%) while AOV stayed flat at ~$72. At 60% gross margin a $72 order yields ~$43 gross profit, so a $61 CAC leaves first-order contribution negative before shipping and returns - the newest customers likely lose money on the first order and must repeat to become profitable.

12-month repeat-purchase rate is declining every cohort: 2022 42%, 2023 35%, 2024 28%. The exact mechanism (the repeats) that is supposed to rescue the negative first-order economics is weakening at the same time CAC rises. The two trends compound against the marginal customer.

~80% of new customers come from two paid platforms with rising CPMs. Doubling spend would push further into the same saturating channels, where marginal CAC typically rises above blended CAC - so the $61 figure likely understates the cost of the next customer at doubled spend. Marginal CAC at scale has not been modeled.
